q: What do terraform state pull and push do, and why is terraform state push dangerous?
p: pull prints the current remote state as JSON, which is safe for inspection and backups. push overwrites the remote state with a local file, bypassing normal checks except a serial and lineage comparison. A wrong push can erase knowledge of real resources.
tip: Take a pull backup before any state surgery, and prefer state mv, rm and import over hand-editing and pushing.
a: State pull downloads the current state from the configured backend and prints it, which is useful for backups, diffing before and after a risky operation, and for scripts that need to inspect it. State push uploads a local file to replace the remote state. Terraform checks the lineage, which identifies the state's history, and the serial number, which increases with every change, and refuses to push an older or unrelated state unless forced. Pushing is dangerous because the state is the only record that maps configuration to real infrastructure. If I overwrite it with a stale or edited copy, Terraform may forget resources, causing duplicates or orphaned infrastructure, or try to recreate things that already exist. I use push only as a last resort for recovery, always with a fresh pull backup, a state lock held, and a review of the diff. For routine changes I use the dedicated commands, or moved and import blocks.
f: What are lineage and serial?
What should you do before state surgery?

q: How do the removed block and terraform state rm differ for taking a resource out of Terraform without destroying it?
p: state rm is an imperative command that forgets a resource immediately. The removed block with lifecycle destroy = false is declarative, reviewable in a pull request, and applied by the normal workflow, so everyone's state is updated consistently.
cmds: removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy lifecycle { destroy = false } }
tip: Declarative blocks leave a code trail and work with remote execution, which is why they beat one-off commands on shared infrastructure.
a: Sometimes I want Terraform to stop managing an object without deleting the real resource, for example when ownership is moving to another team or another state. The older way is the state rm command, which edits the state directly. It works but happens outside review, depends on one person running it against the right workspace, and leaves no history in Git. The newer approach is a removed block in the configuration that names the resource address, with the lifecycle setting that says do not destroy it. When the plan runs, Terraform shows that the resource will be removed from state only, and applying updates the state in a controlled, reviewed way, including in CI and remote runs. I then delete the block after the change is applied everywhere. The same philosophy applies to moved and import blocks, which turn state surgery into code.
f: What does destroy = false do?
When is state rm still acceptable?

q: How do you use terraform plan -generate-config-out to import existing resources, and what review does the generated code need?
p: With an import block that has no matching resource block, plan -generate-config-out writes starter HCL based on the real object's attributes. It is a draft: you must remove computed and default noise, parameterise values, and verify the next plan shows no changes.
tip: The success criterion for any import is a clean plan afterwards, with the config tidy enough to maintain.
a: Importing used to mean writing the resource block by hand, then running import and iterating on plan until the diff disappeared. Now I add an import block with the target address and the real ID, run plan with the generate-config-out option, and Terraform produces a file with a resource block populated from the live object. That saves time, but the output is only a starting point. It often contains every attribute, including read-only ones and defaults, hardcoded values I want as variables, and sometimes conflicting arguments that fail validation. I clean it up, move it into the right module, replace literals with references, and apply to bring the object into state. Then I run another plan to confirm it shows no changes, which proves the configuration matches reality. For bulk imports, I script discovery, generate blocks programmatically, and review in a pull request.
f: Why must the plan be clean after import?
What attributes should you strip from generated config?

q: What is the difference between terraform taint and the -replace option, and why is -replace preferred?
p: taint marks a resource in state as tainted so the next apply recreates it, but modifies state without a plan review. -replace=ADDRESS on plan or apply forces replacement for that run, is visible in the plan, and doesn't change state until applied.
tip: taint is deprecated in favour of -replace because it changes state before anyone has reviewed the consequences.
a: Both approaches are for forcing a healthy-looking resource to be destroyed and recreated, for example a VM with corrupted configuration. The taint command writes a tainted flag into the state, so any later apply, possibly by someone else or by CI, will replace the resource, even though nobody reviewed that in a plan. It is easy to forget a tainted resource and then be surprised. The replace flag is passed to plan or apply for a single run, so the plan clearly shows the resource marked for replacement, the team can review the impact, including dependent resources that may also be recreated, and nothing is stored in state beforehand. If the apply is cancelled, state is not left in an altered condition. That is why the replace option is recommended and taint is deprecated. In an automated pipeline, replacement can also be triggered declaratively with the replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument.
f: What does replace_triggered_by do?
Why can replacement affect dependents?

q: How can large Terraform state files hurt, and what are the signs that it is time to split state?
p: Large state means slow plans and refreshes, long lock times, a big blast radius, noisy diffs, and merge conflicts in review. Signs: plans over several minutes, many unrelated teams editing one root module, and fear of applying. Split by lifecycle, ownership and risk.
cmds: terraform state list | cut -d. -f1-2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
tip: Split along boundaries that change at different rates, such as network, data, platform and applications.
a: The state is read and refreshed on every plan, so thousands of resources mean thousands of API calls and slow feedback. A single lock also means only one person or pipeline can change anything at once, and every apply carries the risk of touching unrelated infrastructure, so a mistake in one area can damage another. I look at warning signs: plan times measured in many minutes, frequent lock contention, engineers afraid to run apply, API rate limit errors, and unrelated teams colliding in one repository. The remedy is to split state along natural boundaries, such as foundational network and identity layers that change rarely, shared platforms, data stores, and individual application stacks that change daily. The layers share information through outputs, remote state or data sources, and I move resources using moved blocks and state migration carefully. Each state should have a clear owner, a permission boundary and a manageable size.
f: How do layers share data?
What is blast radius?

q: What is state encryption in OpenTofu, and how does it differ from backend encryption?
p: OpenTofu can encrypt state and plan files client-side using a key provider such as AWS KMS, GCP KMS or a passphrase, so even someone with read access to the bucket sees ciphertext. Backend encryption (SSE) protects data at rest only from outside the storage service.
cmds: terraform { encryption { key_provider "aws_kms" "main" { kms_key_id = "alias/tf" region = "eu-west-1" } method "aes_gcm" "default" { keys = key_provider.aws_kms.main } state { method = method.aes_gcm.default } } }
tip: Be balanced: mention it is an OpenTofu feature, and that with HashiCorp Terraform you rely on backend encryption and strict access control.
a: State files can contain secrets in plaintext, such as database passwords and private keys. Backend server-side encryption, like S3 with KMS, encrypts the object at rest, but anyone allowed to read the object through the service gets decrypted data, so it protects mainly against theft of the underlying disks. OpenTofu added client-side state and plan encryption: Tofu encrypts the data before sending it to the backend, using a key provider such as a cloud KMS or a passphrase and an algorithm like AES-GCM, so the stored object is ciphertext and reading it requires access to the key as well as the bucket. This provides defence in depth and separates duties. Key management becomes critical, since losing the key means losing the state. With Terraform itself, I rely on backend encryption, tightly scoped IAM, versioning and audit logging, and keep secrets out of state where possible using ephemeral values.
f: What happens if you lose the encryption key?
Why does SSE not stop an authorised reader?

q: How does S3 native state locking (use_lockfile) compare with the DynamoDB lock table?
p: Newer Terraform and OpenTofu versions can lock S3 state using a .tflock object created with conditional writes, removing the need for a DynamoDB table. It simplifies setup and permissions, but you must migrate carefully and make sure all users run supported versions.
cmds: terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "tf-state" key = "prod/network.tfstate" region = "eu-west-1" use_lockfile = true } }
aws s3 ls s3://tf-state/prod/ | grep tflock
tip: During migration you can enable both mechanisms for a while so that older clients still respect the lock.
a: Historically the S3 backend stored state in the bucket and used a DynamoDB table with a lock item to prevent concurrent runs. Recent versions support a lock file stored next to the state object in S3, created with a conditional write so that only one client can succeed. That removes a separate service to provision, secure and pay for, and it reduces the permissions required for the pipeline role. The things to check are the minimum tool versions across every engineer and CI runner, because an older client that only knows DynamoDB would not honour the new lock, which is why a transition period using both can be sensible. Also ensure bucket versioning stays on, the role can write and delete the lock object, and that stuck locks are cleaned up deliberately. I remove the DynamoDB table once every consumer is upgraded and verified.
f: Why keep both locks during migration?
How do you clear a stuck S3 lock?

q: How do remote state backends differ on Google Cloud and Azure, and how is locking handled?
p: The gcs backend stores state in a bucket and uses object generation preconditions for locking. The azurerm backend stores state in a blob container and uses blob leases. Both support encryption, versioning and identity-based auth without keys.
cmds: terraform { backend "azurerm" { resource_group_name = "tf-rg" storage_account_name = "tfstate123" container_name = "state" key = "prod.tfstate" use_oidc = true } }
tip: Turn on object versioning and soft delete so a bad write can be rolled back.
a: Both clouds have first-class object storage backends. On Google Cloud, the gcs backend writes state objects into a bucket, using a prefix to separate states, and handles locking with a lock object that is created with a precondition so concurrent creators fail. On Azure, the azurerm backend stores state as a blob in a container and takes a lease on the blob while an operation runs. Both integrate with native identity, so pipelines authenticate with workload identity federation or managed identities rather than static access keys. For safety I enable versioning or soft delete so earlier state versions can be recovered, restrict the bucket or storage account with IAM to the pipeline identities, turn on encryption with customer-managed keys where policy demands it, enable logging, and block public access. Separate buckets or containers per environment limit the blast radius.
f: How do you recover an older state version?
Why prefer OIDC over keys here?

q: What can go wrong if different team members use different Terraform versions or backend settings, and how do you standardise them?
p: A newer version can upgrade the state format so older versions can no longer read it, providers behave differently, and backend arguments drift. Pin required_version, commit the lock file, use a version manager and run through CI to keep one tool version.
tip: A state written by a newer Terraform may be unreadable by an older one, so one engineer's local apply can block everyone else.
a: Terraform records its version in the state and may change the state format when a newer version writes to it. After that, older versions refuse to read it, so one developer who runs a local apply with a newer binary can break CI and teammates. Provider versions matter too, since a different provider can plan different changes. To avoid this, I set required_version and required_providers constraints, commit the dependency lock file so every machine installs identical provider versions and hashes, store a tool version file read by a version manager such as tfenv or asdf, and run all applies through CI using a container image with a pinned version. Backend configuration is kept in code or in partial config files supplied by the pipeline, not in individual shell history. Upgrades are planned: upgrade the pinned version in a pull request, run plans for every state, then apply during a controlled window.
f: What does the lock file contain?
How do you upgrade Terraform safely across many states?

q: What is Terraform Cloud remote execution versus local execution, and how does it change who needs cloud credentials?
p: With remote execution, plan and apply run on HCP Terraform workers, using credentials and variables stored in the workspace. With local execution the CLI runs on your machine and only state is stored remotely. Remote runs centralise secrets, logs, policy checks and approvals.
cmds: terraform plan   # runs remotely and streams logs
tip: Dynamic provider credentials with OIDC let remote runs assume cloud roles without any stored keys.
a: In remote execution mode, the CLI uploads the configuration to the platform, and the plan and apply run on managed workers. Cloud credentials and sensitive variables live in the workspace, or are obtained dynamically through OIDC federation, so individual engineers do not need production credentials on their laptops. Every run is logged, policy checks run before apply, approvals can be required, and runs are queued so only one runs per workspace at a time. In local execution mode, the workspace is used only as a state backend, and the plan runs wherever the CLI is, using local credentials, which is flexible for debugging but loses centralised control. For production I prefer remote or CI-based execution with short-lived credentials, role-based access on workspaces, and run triggers to chain dependent workspaces, keeping developers on speculative plans for pull requests.
f: What are speculative plans?
What are run triggers?

q: How do you protect Terraform state buckets from deletion, tampering and unauthorised reading?
p: Enable versioning, MFA delete or object lock, bucket policies denying delete except from a break-glass role, block public access, encrypt with KMS, restrict read to pipeline roles, log access, and replicate the bucket for disaster recovery.
tip: Treat the state bucket as tier-zero infrastructure, with its own account and tightly limited administrators.
a: State holds the map of everything Terraform manages and often secrets, so losing or altering it is serious. I protect it in layers. Versioning keeps previous revisions so I can roll back after a bad write or a deletion. Object lock or MFA delete stops even privileged users from permanently removing versions. A bucket policy denies unencrypted uploads and non-TLS access, and denies delete actions to everyone except a controlled break-glass role. Public access blocks are enabled, and the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key with a narrow key policy. Read and write permissions are granted per state path to the specific pipeline roles that need them, so a team cannot read another team's state. Access logging and CloudTrail data events provide an audit trail, replication to another region gives disaster recovery, and the bucket lives in a dedicated, hardened account.
f: Why use a dedicated account for state?
How do you recover from an accidental deletion?

q: How do policy-as-code tools such as OPA Conftest, Sentinel and Checkov fit into a Terraform pipeline?
p: Static scanners like Checkov and tfsec inspect HCL for known misconfigurations. Conftest with OPA evaluates the JSON plan against custom Rego rules. Sentinel does the same inside HCP Terraform. Run them between plan and apply to fail unsafe changes.
cmds: terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
tip: Scanning the plan JSON catches values only known at plan time, which pure source scanning misses.
a: I use a layered approach. Static analysis tools such as Checkov and tfsec read the code and flag known problems, for example an open security group, unencrypted storage or missing logging, and give developers fast feedback in pre-commit hooks and pull requests. But variables, modules and computed values mean the source does not always show what will really be created. So I also evaluate the rendered plan: convert it to JSON and run Open Policy Agent policies with Conftest, or Sentinel in HCP Terraform, to enforce organisation-specific rules such as required tags, allowed regions, instance types and no public buckets. The policies run after plan and before apply, and a failure blocks the pipeline. Rules have severity levels, with soft-fail overrides requiring approval for exceptions. Policies are versioned and tested like code, and they are complemented by cloud-side guardrails such as service control policies as the last line of defence.
f: Why scan the plan as well as the source?
What are soft-mandatory policies?

q: What are ephemeral resources and write-only attributes in recent Terraform, and how do they keep secrets out of state?
p: Ephemeral values exist only during a run and are never stored in plan or state. Write-only attributes accept a value to send to the provider but don't persist it. Together they let you fetch a secret from a vault and set a password without it appearing in state.
cmds: terraform state show aws_db_instance.main | grep -i password
tip: Say it clearly: this reduces secrets in state, but the secret still needs a proper secret manager as its source of truth.
a: For years, any secret passed through Terraform ended up in the state file in plaintext, whether generated by the random provider, read from a data source, or supplied as a variable. Newer Terraform versions introduce ephemeral values: variables, outputs and resources that exist only while a run is in progress and are not written to plan or state. Providers can also expose write-only arguments, which accept a value during apply but never save it. A pattern is to read a secret from a vault with an ephemeral resource and pass it to a write-only password argument on a database, with a version attribute to trigger updates when the secret rotates. That prevents the secret from appearing in state, plan output or logs. It depends on provider support, and the secret still has to be managed and rotated in a proper secrets manager, so I combine it with workload identity and runtime secret retrieval.
f: How do you trigger rotation with a write-only attribute?
What is still stored in state?

q: How do you authenticate Terraform in CI to AWS, Azure or GCP without long-lived keys, and what do you restrict?
p: Use OIDC federation: the CI system presents a short-lived signed token, and the cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials on a role whose trust policy limits repository, branch and environment. Use separate roles for plan (read-mostly) and apply.
tip: Condition the trust on the exact repo and branch or environment. A loose subject claim lets any repo in the organisation assume your role.
a: Static access keys in CI secrets are a standing risk, so I use OpenID Connect federation. The CI platform issues a signed token for each job, identifying the repository, branch and workflow. In the cloud I configure an identity provider that trusts that issuer, and a role, service account or app registration whose trust policy accepts tokens only with specific claims, such as the exact repository and the main branch or a protected environment. The job exchanges the token for temporary credentials that expire within an hour. I split roles by purpose: a plan role that can read state and describe resources, used for pull requests, and an apply role with write permissions that only the protected branch or an approved environment can assume. Permissions are least-privilege and scoped to the resources that stack manages, and assumption events are logged and monitored.
f: Why separate plan and apply roles?
What claims would you trust?

q: How do you use data sources to read secrets from Vault, Secrets Manager or Key Vault, and what are the risks?
p: Data sources read secret values at plan or apply time, but the values are stored in state in plaintext. Safer patterns reference secret ARNs or names and let the application fetch them at runtime, or use ephemeral resources. Never output secrets.
cmds: resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "app" { container_definitions = jsonencode([{ secrets = [{ name = "DB_PASSWORD", valueFrom = aws_secretsmanager_secret.db.arn }] }]) }
tip: Pass the secret's reference to the workload, not its value. Then neither state nor plan holds the secret.
a: A data source for a secret version reads the value from the secret manager during a run. This is convenient, for example to configure a database or a provider, but Terraform stores data source results in state, so the secret ends up in plaintext there, and also may appear in plan output unless marked sensitive. Anyone who can read the state can read the secret. The safer approach is to avoid passing values through Terraform at all. I give the workload an identity and a permission to read the secret, and pass only the secret's ARN or name, for example through the ECS or Kubernetes secret reference mechanism, so the platform injects it at runtime. When a value is unavoidable, I use ephemeral resources or write-only arguments if supported, mark variables and outputs sensitive, lock down state access, and rotate the secret regularly.
f: Why is sensitive = true not enough?
How does ECS inject secrets without Terraform seeing them?

q: How do you verify the supply chain of Terraform providers and modules, including signatures and checksums?
p: The registry provides signed provider releases and the lock file records hashes for each platform. Pin versions, commit the lock, use a private registry or mirror for modules and providers, review module source, and scan dependencies for known issues.
tip: A filesystem or network mirror also protects builds from registry outages and tag changes.
a: Providers are executables that run with your cloud credentials, and modules are code that creates infrastructure, so both are supply chain risks. Terraform verifies provider signatures from the registry and records the checksums of the exact packages in the lock file, so subsequent installs on any machine must match, and I commit that file and generate hashes for every platform used in CI and laptops. I pin exact or tightly bounded versions and update through reviewed pull requests with automation such as Renovate. For modules I pin to immutable versions or commit hashes rather than a branch, prefer modules from the internal private registry that have been reviewed, and read the source of third-party ones for provisioners, external data sources or unexpected resources. Mirroring providers and modules internally gives control over what is available and protects against deletion, and dependency scanning tools check for known vulnerabilities.
f: Why pin modules to commit hashes?
What is a provider mirror?

q: How do you restrict what Terraform itself can do, using IAM permission boundaries and separate roles per stack?
p: Give each state its own role with only the services and resource prefixes it manages, add a permission boundary so it cannot create more powerful roles, deny destructive actions on protected resources, and use SCPs as the outer guardrail.
tip: A Terraform role with AdministratorAccess is effectively a root key stored in CI. Start from last-accessed data and trim.
a: Terraform needs broad permissions to create infrastructure, so the role it uses is a prime target. I avoid one all-powerful role for everything. Each stack or environment has its own role limited to the services it manages and, where possible, to resource name prefixes or tags. A permission boundary caps the maximum permissions of any role Terraform may create, which prevents privilege escalation by creating an admin role. Explicit denies protect critical assets such as audit logs, the state bucket and security tooling. Organization-level service control policies set the outer limits. To size the permissions, I start with generous access in a sandbox, use last accessed data and policy generation to see what is actually used, and tighten. Plan jobs run with a read-only role, and apply jobs run only from the protected branch with approvals. All role usage is logged and alerts fire on unusual actions.
f: What does a permission boundary do?
Why use a read-only role for plan?

q: What are good module composition patterns, and why prefer small focused modules wired together by a root module?
p: Keep modules focused on one capability with a clear input and output contract, compose them in root modules, avoid deep nesting, and don't wrap a single resource without adding value. Pass dependencies explicitly via variables and outputs.
tip: A thin wrapper around one resource is usually a smell. A module should encapsulate a decision or a pattern, not just rename arguments.
a: The best modules represent a meaningful building block, such as a network, a database with its subnet group and parameter group, or a service with its load balancer, and expose a small, stable interface of variables and outputs. The root module wires them together, passing the outputs of one as inputs to another, which makes dependencies explicit and the graph easy to understand. I avoid very deep nesting because it hides where resources come from and makes debugging hard, and avoid passing entire objects or configuration blobs through many layers. Modules should not configure providers internally, they should receive them, and should validate inputs and document outputs. I resist wrapping a single resource just to rename arguments, because that adds indirection with no value. Versioning modules and testing them separately lets teams consume them safely, and composition lets different environments reuse the same blocks.
f: Why shouldn't modules configure providers?
What makes a module interface stable?

q: How do you use for_each and count on modules, and what limitations apply?
p: Modules support count and for_each, creating multiple instances addressed by index or key. Each instance has its own state addresses. Keys must be known at plan time, and changing a key destroys and recreates that instance unless you use moved blocks.
cmds: module "service" { for_each = var.services  source = "./modules/service"  name = each.key  config = each.value }
tip: Use stable keys such as names, not list indexes, so inserting an item does not shift everything.
a: Since Terraform version 0.13, modules accept count and for_each, so I can instantiate the same module for each item in a map or set, for example one per microservice or per environment. Each instance is addressed in state by its key, such as module dot service with the key in brackets, so adding or removing one item affects only that instance. With count, the address is the numeric index, so removing an element in the middle shifts all later indexes and causes unwanted destroy and recreate actions, which is why I prefer for_each with stable keys. The keys must be known at plan time, they cannot depend on values only known after apply, which sometimes forces a two-stage apply or a redesign. Renaming a key looks like a delete and a create, so I add a moved block to preserve the resource. Also, remember that providers can't be passed dynamically per instance in old versions.
f: Why is count risky for lists that change?
What does 'known after apply' break?

q: How does terraform test work, and what can you assert with it?
p: terraform test runs .tftest.hcl files containing run blocks that apply or plan a configuration with given variables and then check assertions on outputs and resources. It can use mock providers for fast unit tests, and real applies for integration tests.
cmds: run "creates_private_subnets" { command = plan variables { cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" } assert { condition = length(aws_subnet.private) == 3 error_message = "expected 3 private subnets" } }
tip: Use command = plan with mock providers for fast, free checks, and reserve real applies for a few key integration paths.
a: Terraform has a built-in test framework. Test files with the tftest extension contain run blocks. Each run block executes either a plan or an apply of the module under test with specific variable values, and then evaluates assert blocks that check conditions on outputs, resource attributes or the number of resources, failing with a clear message. Because tests that apply create real infrastructure and are cleaned up afterwards, I keep them for important integration scenarios in a sandbox account. For quick feedback, I use plan-only runs and mock providers, which simulate provider responses without touching a cloud, to check logic like conditionals, naming and count calculations. Expected failures can be tested with expect_failures for variable validations. I run tests in CI on every pull request for shared modules, and complement them with static analysis and policy checks, while Terratest or Kitchen-style tests remain useful for end-to-end validation of live behaviour.
f: What are mock providers?
How do you test a validation rule?

q: When would you use terraform_data or the null_resource replacement, and what are the alternatives to provisioners?
p: terraform_data is the built-in replacement for null_resource, storing input and triggering replacement on changes with triggers_replace. Provisioners are a last resort; prefer cloud-init or user data, configuration management, images, or the provider's native resources.
tip: HashiCorp documents provisioners as a last resort because they are not declarative and failures leave resources tainted.
a: terraform_data is a built-in resource that needs no provider and can hold a value, expose it as output, and trigger replacement when the value in triggers_replace changes. It replaces the old null_resource from the null provider, with simpler behaviour. It is typically used to attach a provisioner or to create a dependency or change-trigger that has no real cloud object behind it. Provisioners such as local-exec and remote-exec run scripts, but they are imperative, not tracked in state beyond success or failure, and make runs fragile and hard to reproduce. Alternatives are better: cloud-init or user data for instance bootstrap, pre-baked images from Packer, configuration management or Kubernetes operators for software setup, and native provider resources or data sources for the actual capability. When I do need a script, I keep it idempotent, make triggers explicit and treat it as technical debt to remove.
f: Why are provisioners a last resort?
What does triggers_replace do?

q: How do you design module outputs and variable types to keep interfaces stable as modules evolve?
p: Expose only what consumers need, use typed objects with optional attributes and defaults, validate inputs, avoid leaking provider-specific structures, and treat outputs as a public API. Deprecate and version rather than rename or remove abruptly.
cmds: variable "db" { type = object({ engine = string, size = optional(string, "db.t3.medium"), multi_az = optional(bool, true) }) }
variable "env" { type = string validation { condition = contains(["dev","stage","prod"], var.env) error_message = "env must be dev, stage or prod" } }
tip: Adding an optional input or a new output is backward compatible. Renaming or removing one is a breaking change that deserves a major version.
a: A module's variables and outputs are its public API, so I design them as carefully as any library interface. For inputs, I use precise types, with objects and optional attributes with defaults for grouped settings, add validation blocks that fail early with helpful messages, and write descriptions. I keep the number of required inputs small and provide sensible secure defaults. For outputs, I return only what consumers need, such as identifiers, endpoints and ARNs, and avoid dumping the whole resource object, which couples callers to provider internals. Changes follow semantic versioning: adding optional inputs and new outputs is non-breaking, while renaming, removing or changing a type is a major version with a migration guide and, where resource addresses change, moved blocks. Automated tests and examples in the module repository act as documentation and a safety net.
f: What makes a change breaking?
Why avoid returning entire resource objects?

q: What does the provider plugin cache do, and how does it speed up CI?
p: By default every working directory downloads its own copies of providers during init. Setting plugin_cache_dir (or TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR) shares downloaded providers across directories and builds, saving bandwidth and minutes, especially in monorepos with many states.
cmds: terraform init   # second run reuses cached providers
tip: Cache the directory between CI runs, keyed on the lock file hash, to avoid redownloading large providers.
a: The AWS and other large providers can be hundreds of megabytes, and each time init runs in a fresh directory it downloads them again. In a repository with dozens of Terraform roots, or on CI runners that start clean for every job, this wastes a lot of time and bandwidth and can hit registry rate limits. The plugin cache directory solves this: when it is configured, init stores each provider version once and links to it from the working directory. I set the environment variable in the CI image, persist the directory using the CI system's cache keyed by the hash of the lock file, and make sure the lock files exist so that the checksums are verified. For fully offline or restricted environments, a provider mirror gives the same benefit with more control. This is a simple change that often cuts minutes from every pipeline run.
f: How does a provider mirror differ?
What should the CI cache key be?

q: When is -refresh=false safe to use, and what are the risks?
p: -refresh=false skips reading real infrastructure and trusts state, making plans much faster. It is safe when state is known to be fresh, for example in a quick re-plan after a recent apply, but dangerous for detecting drift or in production decisions.
tip: Use it for iteration while developing, but run a full refreshing plan before the final apply.
a: During a normal plan, Terraform calls the provider to read the current state of each resource and updates its in-memory view before computing differences. For large states this is the slowest part, so skipping it with the refresh flag set to false gives much faster plans. The risk is that Terraform then compares configuration to the stored state, not to reality, so if something changed outside Terraform it will not be noticed, and the plan may be wrong: it might try to create something that exists or miss a deletion. I use it when iterating on code in a development environment, or immediately after an apply when I know state is current. For production applies, and for drift checks, I always run a full plan, and I schedule separate refresh-only plans to detect drift. A faster alternative for big configurations is splitting state so full refreshes are smaller.
f: What does refresh-only do?
Why not use refresh=false for production?

q: How can many for_each resources and large data lookups slow Terraform, and how do you design around it?
p: Each instance is a separate graph node and API call set. Thousands of instances, or data sources that run for each, make plans slow and hit API limits. Batch via resources that accept lists, move to separate states, cache lookups with locals, and avoid per-item data sources.
tip: Count API calls with debug logs. The number of requests, not Terraform CPU, is usually the cost driver.
a: Terraform builds a graph with a node per resource instance and refreshes each one. A for_each over a thousand security group rules or DNS records can mean thousands of API reads on every plan, and data sources inside the loop add more, so runtimes grow and rate limits are hit. Ways to design around it are to use resources that manage many items in a single object where the provider supports it, such as a single policy document with many statements, to fetch shared lookups once into a local or a data source outside the loop and index into it, to avoid per-item data sources, and to split very large sets across multiple states or modules by ownership. I can tune parallelism carefully, but the providers' rate limits matter more. Measuring the actual API calls with debug logging helps me find the dominant cost, rather than guessing.
f: What does -parallelism change?
How do provider rate limits show up?

q: What are the pros and cons of Terragrunt for reducing duplication, and when is it worth adopting?
p: Terragrunt wraps Terraform to keep backend and provider configuration DRY, orchestrate dependencies between stacks and run commands across many directories. It adds another tool and abstraction layer, so adopt it when you have many similar stacks and environments.
tip: Alternatives: Terraform workspaces plus modules, Terraform Cloud stacks, or plain CI orchestration. Choose the simplest that fits.
a: Terragrunt is a thin wrapper that generates backend and provider blocks from a shared parent configuration, so each stack directory only needs its inputs, and it understands dependencies between directories so run-all commands apply things in the right order and can pass outputs along. This removes lots of copy-pasted backend settings and makes environments like dev, stage and prod, each with dozens of small states, manageable. The costs are an extra tool and language layer for new team members to learn, harder debugging because errors come through the wrapper, version compatibility to track, and some overlap with newer native features. It pays off when there are many stacks that follow the same pattern across accounts and regions. For small setups, plain Terraform with modules, a clean directory layout and a CI pipeline is simpler. I decide based on the number of states and the team's skills.
f: What does run-all do?
What native features overlap with Terragrunt?

q: How do preconditions, postconditions and check blocks improve safety, and how do they differ?
p: Preconditions and postconditions inside lifecycle blocks fail the run when assumptions about inputs or results are violated. check blocks run assertions, including on data sources, that only warn rather than stop, and are good for ongoing health validation.
cmds: resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = var.ami lifecycle { precondition { condition = data.aws_ami.selected.architecture == "x86_64" error_message = "AMI must be x86_64" } } }
check "site_up" { data "http" "home" { url = "https://example.com" } assert { condition = data.http.home.status_code == 200 error_message = "home page down" } }
tip: Use conditions for assumptions that must hold before or after change, and check blocks for monitoring-style assertions that should not block applies.
a: These features move validation closer to where assumptions are made. A precondition in a resource or data source lifecycle block is evaluated before creating or updating it, so I can verify that a selected AMI has the right architecture or that a subnet belongs to the expected VPC, and fail with a clear message before touching anything. A postcondition is evaluated after, checking that the result meets expectations, for example that a looked-up resource has a required tag, protecting downstream consumers. Both stop the run on failure. A check block is different: it contains assertions and optional scoped data sources, evaluated at the end of plan and apply, and failures appear as warnings without blocking, which is suited to verifying that a deployed endpoint responds or a certificate is not close to expiry. Variable validation covers simple input rules, and together these make configurations self-checking.
f: Variable validation versus preconditions?
Why not block on a check failure?

q: How do prevent_destroy and ignore_changes work, and what are their pitfalls?
p: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail, a guard against accidents, but it blocks legitimate destroys until removed. ignore_changes tells Terraform to disregard drift in listed attributes, useful for fields changed by other systems, but it can hide real problems.
tip: Use ignore_changes narrowly on named attributes, never on whole blocks, and leave a comment explaining who else changes them.
a: The lifecycle block lets me adjust Terraform's behaviour for a resource. Setting prevent_destroy to true makes Terraform error out if a plan would destroy that resource, including a replacement, which protects databases and state buckets from accidental removal. The pitfalls are that it only applies while the code is present, since deleting the resource block also deletes the protection, and it can obstruct intentional teardown, so people sometimes remove it casually. It should be backed by deletion protection on the cloud resource itself and by IAM. ignore_changes tells Terraform not to react to differences in specific attributes. That is appropriate for fields managed elsewhere, such as an autoscaler adjusting desired capacity or a security tool adding tags. Used too broadly it hides drift that matters, so I list exact attributes, document why, and review them periodically.
f: Why also enable deletion protection on the resource?
What happens if you delete the resource block?

q: What does create_before_destroy do, and what problems can it cause with unique names?
p: It creates the replacement before destroying the old resource, giving zero-downtime replacement for things like launch templates, certificates and load balancer listeners. If the resource has a unique name, both can't exist at once, so use name_prefix or random suffixes.
cmds: terraform plan | grep -E 'must be replaced|create replacement'
tip: The setting propagates to dependencies, so resources the replaced one depends on may also be forced into create-before-destroy.
a: By default, when a change forces replacement, Terraform destroys the old object first and then creates the new one, which causes downtime if something depends on it. With create_before_destroy the order is reversed: the new object is created, dependants are updated to point to it, and then the old one is removed. That suits certificates, launch templates, security groups and instances behind load balancers. The common problem is name collisions: if the resource must have a unique name, the replacement cannot be created while the old exists, so I use name_prefix to let the provider generate unique names, or add a random suffix that changes with the replacement trigger. Another subtlety is that the flag is inherited by upstream dependencies, which can lead to unexpected duplicates and quota usage, and some resources, like those with unique constraints on IP or port, cannot support it.
f: Why does name_prefix help?
What quota issues can arise?

q: What does replace_triggered_by do, and how do you use it to roll dependent resources?
p: replace_triggered_by makes a resource be replaced whenever a referenced resource or attribute changes. It is useful when something must be recreated to pick up a change that Terraform wouldn't otherwise see, like instances after a launch template or secret version change.
cmds: resource "aws_instance" "app" { ami = var.ami lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [aws_launch_template.app.latest_version, terraform_data.config_version] } }
tip: Pair it with terraform_data holding a version value so you can force a controlled roll by bumping one variable.
a: Sometimes a resource needs to be rebuilt because something it depends on changed, but the dependency is not in an argument that triggers replacement. For example, a running instance does not change when a launch template gets a new version, or a container is not restarted when a secret version changes. The replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument lists resources or attributes, and when any of them is updated or replaced, Terraform plans a replacement of this resource too. I use it for rolling instances after a configuration change, recreating a job after a schema change, or tying replacement to a version number held in terraform_data so I can trigger it deliberately. It must be used carefully, because it can cascade into large replacements, and I check the plan to see the full set of resources affected. Combining it with create_before_destroy limits downtime.
f: What references are allowed?
How do you limit cascading replacements?

q: How do you design blue-green or canary infrastructure changes with Terraform, for example a new Kubernetes node group or database version?
p: Create the new stack alongside the old, shift traffic gradually via weighted DNS, load balancer rules or target groups, verify health, then retire the old. Control the shift with variables or separate applies, and keep the rollback path as a one-variable change.
cmds: resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "canary" { action { type = "forward" forward { target_group { arn = aws_lb_target_group.blue.arn weight = 100 - var.green_weight } target_group { arn = aws_lb_target_group.green.arn weight = var.green_weight } } } }
tip: Treat destroying the old environment as a separate, later change, after the observation window passes.
a: Terraform is declarative, so zero-downtime strategies come from how I model the infrastructure. For blue-green, I define both environments, often as two instances of the same module with different version inputs, and put a traffic switch in front: weighted target groups on a load balancer, weighted DNS records, or a service mesh route. A variable controls the weight, so a pull request that moves ten percent, then fifty, then one hundred percent to green is small and reviewable, and rollback is changing the variable back. I validate health checks and metrics between steps. Only after an observation period do I remove the old environment in a separate change. For stateful resources such as databases, replacement is risky, so I prefer replicas, blue-green features of the managed service or migration tooling, with lifecycle protections and backups. The key is making each step reversible.
f: Why destroy the old stack in a separate change?
How do you handle databases in blue-green?

q: How do you handle the Terraform lifecycle when a provider defaults or API behaviour change and cause perpetual diffs?
p: Identify the attribute that differs between config and state, check provider changelogs and issues, set the value explicitly to match the API's normalised form, use ignore_changes as a targeted workaround, or upgrade the provider that fixes it.
tip: Common culprits are normalised JSON policy documents, case differences, ordering of lists and sets, and defaults the provider fills in.
a: A perpetual diff happens when each plan shows a change that applying never fixes. I run plan and read exactly which attribute differs, then compare the value in configuration with the value in state. Frequent causes are an API that normalises what I send, for example reordering or lower-casing values, JSON policies with different whitespace or key order, a provider default that is filled in when I leave an argument empty, and sets or lists whose order changes. The fix is to write the configuration in the canonical form, use jsonencode or policy document data sources for JSON, specify the defaulted value explicitly, or switch from a list to a set. If the provider has a bug, I look for an issue and a fixed version, and as a workaround use ignore_changes on that specific attribute, with a comment linking the issue. A noisy plan trains people to ignore diffs, so I treat it as a bug.
f: Why do JSON policies cause diffs?
When is ignore_changes acceptable here?

q: How does Atlantis work for pull-request automation, and what are its security considerations?
p: Atlantis listens to pull request webhooks, runs terraform plan when code changes and posts the output, then runs apply when a reviewer comments atlantis apply. It holds credentials and executes arbitrary code, so restrict who can trigger it, require approvals, and isolate workers.
cmds: atlantis.yaml: projects: - name: prod dir: environments/prod apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]
tip: Anyone who can open a pull request can make Atlantis run code with its cloud credentials, so repo access equals credential access.
a: Atlantis is a self-hosted server that connects to the version control system. When a pull request changes Terraform files, it automatically runs plan for the affected projects and comments the output on the pull request. After review, an authorised person comments to apply, and Atlantis runs the apply, locks the project to avoid conflicts and then the change is merged. The advantages are visibility, locking and a consistent execution environment. The security considerations are significant: the server runs Terraform code from pull requests with real cloud credentials, and a malicious change, for example an external data source or provisioner, can exfiltrate those credentials during plan. So I restrict which repositories and users can trigger runs, require approvals and passing checks before apply, use least-privilege credentials per project, run workers in isolated network segments with ephemeral workspaces, and protect the webhook secret and server access.
f: Why can a plan be dangerous?
How does Atlantis locking work?

q: How do you add cost estimation with Infracost to a Terraform pull request workflow?
p: Infracost reads the plan or code, prices resources with cloud pricing data, and posts a diff of monthly cost on the pull request. Teams set thresholds and policies so large increases need approval, building cost awareness into review.
tip: Usage-based costs, such as data transfer or requests, need usage estimates in a config file, or they will be underreported.
a: Cost problems are cheapest to fix before deployment. Infracost runs in the pipeline, parses the Terraform plan or configuration, matches resources to public price lists, and calculates monthly cost. It compares against the base branch and comments the difference on the pull request, for example a new instance type or a bigger database adds a certain amount. Reviewers see cost next to the code diff. I add policies, such as requiring approval from finance or a platform lead when the monthly increase exceeds a threshold, and tag resources so costs map to teams after deployment. The limitations are that estimates cover only resources whose prices it knows, usage-based items like data transfer, requests and storage growth require assumptions supplied in a usage file, and reserved pricing or discounts may not be reflected. So I treat the numbers as directional and reconcile against actual billing regularly.
f: Why are usage-based costs hard to estimate?
What threshold would you set for approvals?

q: How do you securely store, pass and verify the saved plan file between plan and apply jobs in CI?
p: Write the plan with -out, store it as a protected artifact (encrypted, short retention, access-limited), and apply exactly that file so what was reviewed is what runs. The plan can contain secrets, so treat it like state.
tip: If the state changes between plan and apply, Terraform refuses the stale plan, which is the safety you want.
a: The point of a saved plan is to guarantee that apply performs exactly what was reviewed. The plan job writes the plan to a file, publishes a human-readable summary for reviewers, and uploads the file as an artifact. The apply job downloads that exact artifact, optionally verifies a checksum recorded earlier, and runs apply on it with no further prompts. If anything changed in the state in between, Terraform detects the mismatch and refuses to apply, which forces a fresh plan. Because plan files can contain sensitive values, I store them in encrypted storage with limited access, short retention, and never attach them to public logs or pull request comments. The same version of Terraform and providers must be used in both jobs, which I enforce with the same container image and lock file. Approvals sit between the jobs for protected environments.
f: Why must tool versions match between jobs?
What happens if state changes after the plan?

q: How do you detect and alert on Terraform drift on a schedule, and what do you do when drift is found?
p: Run scheduled refresh-only plans with -detailed-exitcode in CI for each state. Exit code 2 means differences. Notify the owning team with the diff, then decide: revert the manual change by applying, or adopt it into code via a reviewed pull request.
tip: Classify drift: benign (autoscaler fields), risky (security groups) and malicious (IAM). Route alerts accordingly.
a: I schedule a pipeline, for example nightly, that runs a refresh-only plan for every state using a read-only role, with the detailed exit code option so a result of two means there are differences. When drift is found, the job posts the diff to the owning team's channel with a link to the run. The team then decides what is right. If the change was an unauthorised or accidental console edit, I reapply the code to restore the intended state. If the change was legitimate, such as an emergency fix, I update the code through a pull request so the code and reality match, and then the plan returns to clean. Benign fields changed by other systems are excluded with ignore_changes. I also reduce drift at the source by restricting console write access, using service control policies, and logging who made changes. Trend reports show which stacks drift most.
f: What does exit code 2 mean?
How do you reduce drift at the source?

q: How do you structure a reusable GitHub Actions or GitLab pipeline for Terraform across many repositories?
p: Create a shared, versioned reusable workflow or template that does fmt, validate, scan, plan and apply with standard guards, called from each repo with a few inputs. Central control means improvements and security fixes roll out everywhere through version bumps.
cmds: terraform fmt -check -recursive && terraform validate && tflint && checkov -d .
tip: Pin the shared workflow to a tag or commit and update it deliberately, because it runs with your cloud credentials.
a: Duplicating pipeline YAML in dozens of repositories leads to drift, forgotten security steps and painful upgrades. Instead, the platform team maintains a reusable workflow, or a GitLab include template, that encapsulates the standard stages: format check, validate, linting, security scans, plan with a comment on the pull request, policy checks, and an apply job gated on the main branch and environment approvals. Each repository calls it with a few inputs such as the working directory, the role to assume and variables. Credentials come from OIDC, not stored secrets. The shared workflow is versioned with tags, consumers pin a version, and updates are rolled out through automated pull requests with release notes. This gives consistent guardrails, easier audits and one place to improve caching, concurrency controls, and notifications. Exceptions are handled through inputs, not forks.
f: Why pin the reusable workflow version?
How do you roll out a pipeline change to 50 repos?

q: terraform apply fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock' and the lock info shows a run from hours ago. What do you do?
p: First prove no apply is running (check CI, ask the owner, read lock info). If it is stale, use terraform force-unlock with the lock ID. Then run plan to verify state integrity, and handle any partially applied changes.
tip: Forcing an unlock during a live apply can corrupt state, so verification comes first.
a: The error includes the lock ID, who holds it, the operation, the time and the version. I check whether that operation is really still running: look at the CI job, ask the person named in the lock, and check whether the process or runner still exists. Locks become stale when a job is killed, a laptop sleeps, or a network connection drops. If I am confident nothing is running, I release it with force-unlock and the lock ID, or for the S3 lock file backend by removing the lock object, and for DynamoDB by deleting the item. Then I run a plan and inspect the result carefully, because the interrupted run may have created some resources without recording them. If state is missing resources, I import them, and if there is any doubt I restore a previous state version from bucket versioning. Afterwards, I prevent cancelling apply jobs in CI and add alerts for locks held longer than normal.
f: How do you tell if a run is still active?
Why avoid cancelling apply jobs?

q: After an apply you see 'Provider produced inconsistent result after apply'. What does it mean and how do you recover?
p: The provider returned a value different from what the plan predicted, a provider bug or eventual consistency issue. The resource may exist but state may be tainted or partial. Re-run plan, check the real object, refresh or import, and upgrade or report the provider.
tip: This is almost always a provider bug, not user error, so check the issue tracker and try a newer or older provider version.
a: Terraform computes a plan with expected values, applies it through the provider, and then checks that the values returned match what was promised. When they do not, for example an attribute was planned as one value and the API returned another, or an unknown value resolved differently, Terraform reports that the provider produced an inconsistent result. It indicates a bug in the provider or an API that changes data asynchronously. The resource might have been created, and state may record it as tainted or partially filled. I run another plan to see what Terraform believes, look at the real object in the console, and often a refresh-only apply or a simple re-apply fixes the state, since the second run sees the real value. If it keeps happening, I search the provider's issue tracker, try a different provider version, or add a workaround such as ignore_changes. I also report the issue with reproduction steps.
f: Why does Terraform verify results after apply?
How would you report a provider bug?

q: Terraform fails with 'Cycle: ...' errors. How do you find and break the dependency cycle?
p: Two or more resources reference each other, directly or through intermediaries, so no valid order exists. Read the cycle path in the error, use terraform graph to visualise, and break it by splitting a resource, using separate rule resources, or moving the shared value into a data source or variable.
tip: The classic case is two security groups referencing each other inline. Use aws_security_group_rule resources instead.
a: Terraform builds a directed acyclic graph from references between resources, and if A depends on B and B depends on A, directly or through a longer chain, there is no valid order and it reports a cycle with the list of involved objects. I read the error, which names the nodes, and visualise the graph around them if needed. The usual causes are two security groups that each reference the other in inline rules, a resource that uses an output of something that itself depends on it through a provisioner or a module output, or an overuse of depends_on. To break the cycle I separate the part that creates the circular reference from the creation of the object: for security groups, create both groups first and then add the rules as standalone rule resources, or use a data source or variable instead of a direct reference. I then re-validate and check the plan order.
f: Why do inline security group rules cause cycles?
What does depends_on add to the graph?

q: for_each fails with 'The for_each value depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply'. How do you fix it?
p: for_each keys must be known at plan time. Build keys from static values or inputs, not from attributes of resources not yet created. Use a stable map keyed by names, split the apply with -target as a last resort, or restructure into two layers.
cmds: for_each = { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }
tip: Keys must be known; values can be unknown. Use human-chosen names as keys and the unknown ID as the value.
a: To plan instance addresses, Terraform must know the set of keys for for_each before anything is created. If I derive the keys from something computed during apply, such as the IDs of subnets that are being created in the same run, it cannot do that and fails. The fix is to design the keys to come from static information: variable inputs, names I choose, or values known at plan time. For example, key the map by a logical name such as the availability zone or role, and use the unknown ID only in the values, which are allowed to be unknown. If the structure truly depends on infrastructure that does not exist yet, I split the configuration into layers so the first creates the dependencies and the second reads them as data, or as a last resort do a targeted first apply, which I document and avoid in automation. Count has the same rule for its number.
f: Why can values be unknown but keys cannot?
What is a two-layer apply?

q: A tag or name change makes Terraform want to replace a production resource. How do you avoid the replacement?
p: Check which attribute forces replacement in the plan. If it is only metadata you want to keep, restore the old value, use ignore_changes, rename in place if the provider supports it, or use moved and lifecycle controls. Never apply a surprise replacement of stateful resources.
tip: Read the (forces replacement) marker. It tells you exactly which argument is immutable on the provider side.
a: The plan marks the attribute that forces replacement. For many resources, names and identifiers are immutable in the cloud API, so changing them means destroy and create. I first ask whether the change is intended. If someone refactored a naming convention in a shared module, the right action is often to revert the value for existing resources, adding a variable to preserve the legacy name. If the provider supports in-place rename through a different argument, I use that. Where a field is managed elsewhere, ignore_changes can suppress the diff. For stateful resources like databases, I add prevent_destroy and deletion protection so plan fails loudly. If replacement is genuinely needed, I plan a migration: create the new resource, copy data, switch consumers, and then remove the old one, possibly importing or using moved blocks. I never merge a plan that unexpectedly destroys production data.
f: Why do names often force replacement?
How do you migrate data before replacing?

q: A secret ended up in the Terraform state and in plan output in CI logs. What is your response?
p: Rotate the secret immediately, remove it from logs where possible, restrict who can read state and logs, then fix the root cause by using sensitive values, ephemeral or write-only attributes, runtime secret references, and log masking. Audit access to the state and logs.
cmds: terraform state pull | jq '.. | objects | select(has("password"))' | head
tip: Rotation matters more than cleanup. Assume anyone who could read the logs or state has the secret.
a: First I treat the secret as compromised and rotate it at its source, updating consumers. Cleaning up logs and state is secondary, because copies may exist in artifacts, caches and backups. Next I assess exposure: who could read the CI logs and the state bucket, including old object versions, and what access logs show about reads. I redact or delete log entries where the platform allows, and remove old state versions that contain the secret if policy permits. Then I fix the cause. I mark variables and outputs as sensitive so they are masked in output, move secrets out of Terraform by passing references to a secret manager and letting workloads fetch at runtime, use write-only and ephemeral features where available, mask values in CI, and avoid printing plans with unredacted values. I add pipeline scanning for secrets in code, tighten state access to pipeline roles, and write up lessons learned.
f: Why is rotation more important than log cleanup?
How do you mask secrets in CI logs?

q: Apply fails halfway because of an account quota or service limit error. How do you proceed safely?
p: Terraform records what was created, so state reflects the partial progress. Request the quota increase or reduce the change, then re-run plan and apply to finish. Check for resources created but not recorded, and avoid destroying the half-built stack.
tip: Check quotas in the plan phase with a pre-flight script for big launches, so you do not discover limits mid-apply.
a: A failure in the middle of apply does not undo earlier steps, and Terraform writes the state for everything that succeeded, so the right move is usually to fix the cause and run apply again, not destroy. I read the error to identify the limit, for example number of vCPUs, elastic IPs or load balancers per region. I request a quota increase through the service quotas API or support, or change the plan to stay within the limit, perhaps by using a different region or instance family. While waiting I run a plan to see what remains, and confirm that no resource was created in the cloud but missing from state, which can occur if the provider crashed after creating something, and import it if so. Then I apply again, which creates the remaining resources. To prevent surprises, I check quotas before large rollouts, request increases in advance, and monitor quota usage with alarms.
f: What if a resource is created but not in state?
How do you pre-check quotas?

q: Terraform says a resource 'already exists' on create, such as an S3 bucket, IAM role or DNS record. How do you handle it?
p: The object exists in the cloud but not in your state, from a manual creation, another stack, a previous partial apply or a failed state write. Decide who owns it: import it into this state, rename yours, or remove the duplicate. Avoid deleting without checking ownership.
tip: Search other states first. Two stacks managing the same object will fight forever.
a: The cloud API is telling me that the name or identifier is already taken. Before acting, I find out who created it. If it was created by hand, or by an earlier apply that failed to save state, and this configuration is meant to own it, I import it, via an import block or the import command, and then run a plan to see any differences between the configuration and the object and decide whether to adjust the code or let Terraform change the resource. If another Terraform state already manages it, I must not import it in a second place; instead I decide which stack owns it and reference it with a data source from the other. If it is an unrelated object with a clashing name, I rename mine, especially for globally unique names such as buckets. I avoid deleting the existing object until I understand what depends on it, and update the documentation on ownership.
f: Why must one object have one owning state?
How do you find which state manages an object?

q: A provider major upgrade breaks many plans, for example the AWS provider splitting S3 bucket arguments into separate resources. How do you migrate safely?
p: Read the upgrade guide, pin the old version, upgrade in a branch, run plans per state to see diffs, refactor configuration to the new resource model, import or move where needed so no infrastructure is replaced, then roll out environment by environment.
cmds: terraform show -json upgrade.plan | jq '[.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions|index("delete"))] | length'
tip: The success criterion is a plan with no destroys, and ideally no changes at all, before any real apply.
a: I start with the provider's upgrade guide and changelog to understand breaking changes, such as arguments removed from a resource and moved into a standalone resource. I keep production pinned to the old version while working in a branch with a non-production state copy. Upgrading the lock file and running plan reveals the impact per state. My goal is no destroys and no replacements: I refactor the code to the new structure, and where new resource types need to take over management of existing settings, I import them or use import blocks so that state matches reality. Modules shared by many stacks are updated and versioned first, then consumers. I check the count of destroy actions in plan JSON as an automated gate. Rollout proceeds from development to production with applies, and I keep a rollback plan of pinning the previous provider version and restoring state backups if something goes wrong.
f: How do you automate the no-destroy gate?
Why upgrade shared modules first?

q: Two pipelines applied to the same state at nearly the same time and one failed or overwrote the other. How do you prevent concurrent applies?
p: Locking prevents simultaneous writes if configured, but queued or retried jobs can still race on stale plans. Use CI concurrency groups per state, one apply per environment at a time, saved plans that fail when state changed, and no manual local applies.
cmds: terraform apply tfplan   # fails with 'Saved plan is stale' if state changed
tip: Never set cancel-in-progress to true for apply jobs. Cancelling mid-apply is how stale locks and partial state happen.
a: Backend locking stops two runs from writing state at the same time, but a race can still occur if a misconfigured backend has no locking, or when a second job queues behind the first, then runs a plan that was computed earlier against older state. I fix it in layers. The backend must support locking and it must be enabled, which I verify by testing. In CI, I define a concurrency group per state or environment so only one apply job runs at a time and others wait, and I set it to queue rather than cancel running jobs. Applying a saved plan means a stale plan is rejected if the state changed meanwhile. I forbid local applies to shared states by removing write credentials from individuals and permitting only the pipeline role. Atlantis or HCP Terraform provide queueing and locks natively. Finally, I make sure deploy jobs have timeouts and clear failure handling.
f: Why queue instead of cancel apply jobs?
What does a stale plan error mean?

q: Terraform init or plan fails with 403 or AccessDenied against the state backend after a role or bucket policy change. How do you debug it?
p: Identify which identity Terraform used and which action was denied. S3 needs list on the bucket, get and put on the object, and KMS permissions; locking needs lockfile or DynamoDB rights. Compare the policy simulator results and CloudTrail denial events.
cmds: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role> --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject kms:Decrypt --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::tf-state/prod/network.tfstate
tip: KMS key policies are a frequent hidden cause. The role can read the object but cannot decrypt it.
a: I first confirm which identity Terraform is actually using, because the wrong profile, an expired session or a changed role trust policy gives surprising results. Then I identify the failing API call from the error message or CloudTrail. The S3 backend needs permission to list the bucket, read and write the state object, and, if used, to create and delete the lock object or items in the lock table. If the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key, the role also needs permission to use that key for encrypt and decrypt, and the key policy must allow it, which is easy to overlook after a policy tightening. Bucket policies with explicit denies, VPC endpoint restrictions or condition keys such as source IP and organization ID may also block requests from the CI runner's network. The policy simulator and the CloudTrail event details point to the denying statement, which I then fix with least privilege.
f: Why does the KMS key policy matter?
How can a VPC endpoint policy cause 403?

q: A data source returns multiple results or none, causing 'Your query returned no results' or 'multiple results' errors. How do you make lookups robust?
p: Make filters specific and deterministic, use most_recent or unique identifiers, or avoid fuzzy lookups for critical resources by passing IDs explicitly. Add preconditions to fail clearly and pin inputs such as AMI IDs through a managed source.
cmds: data "aws_ami" "app" { most_recent = true owners = ["123456789012"] filter { name = "name" values = ["app-*"] } filter { name = "tag:release" values = [var.release] } }
tip: Moving AMI selection to an SSM parameter or explicit variable makes rollbacks possible, whereas most_recent changes under you.
a: Data sources that search by attributes are fragile: an extra match in the account, a deleted image, or a naming change turns into a failed plan, or worse, silently chooses a different object. For lookups that should return exactly one item, I use precise filters, such as owner account, a release tag, and a specific name pattern, and set most_recent only when that is the real intent. For critical dependencies like AMIs, I prefer passing an explicit ID or reading it from a controlled source such as an SSM parameter that the image pipeline updates, so changes are deliberate and reversible, rather than letting the next plan pick whatever is newest. I add preconditions to verify properties of the result and produce readable errors. In modules I often accept the ID as an input and keep the lookup in the root module. Where the object belongs to another Terraform state, an output or remote state reference is more reliable than searching.
f: Why is most_recent risky for AMIs?
When use remote state over a data source?

q: Someone applied against the wrong workspace or account and changed production while intending dev. How do you recover, and how do you prevent it?
p: Stop further applies, assess the damage using the plan and cloud audit logs, restore or revert via a corrective apply or state backup, communicate. Prevent by separate backends and credentials per environment, no shared default workspace, account guards, and CI-only applies.
tip: allowed_account_ids on the provider aborts the run if the credentials point to the wrong account, a cheap and effective guard.
a: First I stop anyone else from applying, then work out exactly what changed using the apply log, the state versions and cloud audit logs. If resources were modified, I decide whether to revert by applying the correct configuration to the affected environment, or to restore a previous state version and reconcile. If something was destroyed, I restore from backups or recreate and import. I communicate quickly with stakeholders and run a blameless review. The deeper issue is that the design allowed one command to reach multiple environments. I prevent it by using separate state backends and separate cloud accounts per environment, with credentials that only work for one, so a developer's default login cannot touch production at all. The provider setting for allowed account IDs aborts if credentials mismatch. Workspaces alone are weak isolation. Production changes go only through the pipeline with approvals, and prompts show the environment.
f: Why are workspaces weak isolation?
What does allowed_account_ids do?

q: A policy check blocks your pull request for a rule you believe is a false positive. How should exceptions be handled?
p: Verify whether it is truly a false positive, then handle the exception transparently: a documented, scoped suppression in code with justification and expiry, approved by the policy owner, tracked, and re-reviewed. Don't disable the check globally or bypass the pipeline.
cmds: #checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_18: access logs go to central log bucket, ticket SEC-1234
tip: Good exceptions have an owner, a reason, a ticket and an expiry date, and are visible in code review.
a: I first investigate whether the finding is truly wrong: read the rule's intent, check the resource's real configuration, and consider whether another control already covers the risk. If it is a genuine false positive or an accepted risk, I follow the exception process rather than bypassing the pipeline. In code, I add a narrowly scoped inline suppression for that specific resource and rule with a comment that gives the justification and a ticket reference, so reviewers see it in the diff. The security or policy owner approves it, and where the policy engine supports it, the exception has an expiry date so it is revisited. I never turn off the rule across the repository or make the check non-blocking to get a merge through. If the same false positive appears repeatedly, I propose improving the rule or the module default. Exceptions are reported periodically to track risk.
f: Why should exceptions expire?
How do you improve a noisy rule?

q: HCP Terraform or your CI runs are stuck in 'pending' or queued for a long time. What do you check?
p: Another run on the same workspace holds the queue or lock, a run is waiting for confirmation, an agent pool has no available agents, run triggers chain upstream runs, or organisation concurrency limits are reached. Inspect the run queue and agent status.
tip: Check for a plan waiting for manual approval first. It blocks everything behind it in the workspace queue.
a: In HCP Terraform, each workspace processes one run at a time in order, so a run waiting for manual approval, a failed plan that has not been discarded, or a long apply blocks the runs behind it. I look at the workspace run list for the head of the queue and what it is waiting for. If runs use self-hosted agents, I check that agents are online, have capacity and match the pool, because an empty pool leaves runs pending indefinitely. Run triggers can chain workspaces, so an upstream failure or pending run delays dependents. Organisation-level concurrency limits on the plan can also queue runs. In a CI system the equivalent causes are concurrency groups, no available runners, or a stuck job holding the group. I resolve it by approving or discarding the blocking run, scaling the agents or runners, and I set auto-discard and timeouts to avoid recurrence. Alerts on queue age catch issues early.
f: Why does one run block the workspace?
How would you scale self-hosted agents?

q: You must split a monolithic Terraform state into three smaller ones without recreating anything. Walk through the process.
p: Back up state, create new roots and backends, move resource addresses with terraform state mv -state-out or moved/import blocks, replace cross-references with outputs and remote state or data sources, and verify each new root shows a clean plan before decommissioning the old config.
cmds: terraform plan   # in each root, expect: No changes
tip: Freeze changes during the migration, and make the old root's plan show no destroys at each step before moving on.
a: I begin with preparation: freeze changes, take a backup of the state, and map which resources belong to which new stack based on lifecycle and ownership, such as network, data and applications. I create the new root modules with their own backends and copy the relevant configuration, replacing direct references to resources in other stacks with outputs consumed through remote state or data sources. Then I move the resource entries. Using state move with an output state file, or import blocks into the new state followed by removed blocks in the old, I transfer each group without touching real infrastructure. After every move I run a plan in both the old and the new root, expecting no changes and certainly no creates or destroys. I move the groups in dependency order, starting with the lowest layer. Once all stacks are clean, I delete the leftover configuration, update the pipelines, permissions and documentation, and keep the backup until the new setup has run successfully for a while.
f: Why move in dependency order?
How do import blocks help with splits?
